Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

items.title: The best pay leaders don’t want to run HR
items.summary:
A few months ago I was on a Zoom call with two business-unit CFOs at a company with 100,000 employees. They had just paid a big consulting firm to look at their pricing. The firm found the company was charging less than its own strategy called for. Fixing that added a point or two of margin, and the consulting project paid for itself.

So then I asked: Would you do the same thing for pay?

A long pause. Shrugs. Then one of them said, “Everybody believes we’re making the right ‘people’ decisions. Nothing is obviously broken.”

It almost always is broken. Just not in ways executives can see until someone adds it all up.

Pay is one of the biggest costs a company has. Most companies have a pay strategy on paper: where they want to land against the market, how they use salary ranges, what they say they reward. The finance department watches the total. It knows whether department leaders came in on budget with headcount projections. But the individual decisions behind it (offers, raises, bonuses, promotions) leak millions per year. And under new right-to-information and pay-transparency laws, pay that drifts from the agreed-upon strategy one decision at a time gets awfully hard to explain.

In the data we’ve analyzed so far, about 6% of accepted offers land outside the company’s own ranges, and one company was at 16%. At one company the written policy says offer around the middle of the band; only 19% of hires landed there. Often there’s a good reason. It just isn’t written down anywhere so nobody can explain it.

Added up, though, that’s money walking out the door, and it…
items.t: The best pay leaders don’t want to run HR

items.title: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
items.summary:
Good morning. Intuit is unwinding its biggest acquisition while betting AI can help it win customers without owning the marketing platform it once viewed as central to that effort.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit ( No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

Mailchimp sale marks strategic shift 

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as…
items.t: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy

items.title: Collective[i] cofounder: 76% of executives think their companies are AI leaders. Only 10% are
items.summary:
Anthropic filed its public S-1 on October 26, 2026 to list on Nasdaq under ticker ANT. The roadshow started November 9. The debut is before Thanksgiving. The valuation is landing around $1.5 trillion, down from a $2 trillion target floated in October. That is a four-year-old company running a $68 billion annualized revenue rate, with $331 billion in stock awards on the balance sheet and about 1,500 employees. Early engineers walk into tens of millions each the day the stock prints.

It is the third major AI exit in H2 2026. SpaceX acquired Cursor for $60 billion in August. AMD bought Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2 billion in September. Anthropic goes public this month at $1.5 trillion. Roughly $1.57 trillion of AI value in ninety days, and the next tier has not filed. Every category where an AI model can eat the layer below it is funded, hiring, and shipping.

The median S&P 500 board is debating whether to renew Salesforce because the vendor added “Claudeforce” to the slide. That debate is the K. Economist Peter Atwater coined the term in 2020 for the pandemic recovery that split one economy into two. Six years later it is the cleanest frame for what AI is doing to corporate America. One side rebuilds the operating substrate. The other buys AI stickers and calls it done.

This piece pulls together a year of writing. The SaaS Debt Trap is the top eating the bottom. The Hypothesis Company is how an AI-first org thinks. 50x Faster is how it ships. Agent Swarm is how it scales. Own the Harness is what it owns. The Quiet Veto is why most leaders stall. The Anthropic IPO is…

items.title: JPMorgan pegs the U.S. grid fix at $1 trillion. A new study says a transformer shortage could stall it
items.summary:
A string of technology failures over the past week grounded flights, delayed bank transactions and knocked out email for millions of Americans, putting the country’s infrastructure vulnerabilities squarely in the spotlight.

The power grid has its own weak spot, and it’s made of copper and steel.

The U.S. could begin running short of the equipment that connects new power plants and data centers to the grid as early as next year, according to a new Johns Hopkins University study published in Cell Reports Sustainability . The researchers found that shortages of transformers and converters would become acute by 2030.

For businesses and households, that likely means higher electricity bills and more frequent power outages.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins associate professor who conducted the study with PhD candidate Boyu Yao, said in a university release. “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry.”

Those cracks are widening fast. U.S. power use, which historically grew about 1% to 2% a year, is projected to climb 21% by 2030 as AI data centers, electric vehicles and broader electrification pile on, according to the study. Data centers alone could account for as much as two-thirds of the expected equipment shortfall. Over the longer run, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association projects U.S. electricity demand will…
items.t: JPMorgan pegs the U.S. grid fix at $1 trillion. A new study says a transformer shortage could stall it

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO is a bellwether—and a warning
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: Is the creator of Claude worth it? 

The big leadership story: A tariff refund boosts Target’s profits. 

The markets: Down globally as Anthropic’s debut fails to improve market sentiment. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Anthropic just pulled off a record-breaking IPO , with the five-year-old company debuting at a value of $2 trillion. Is the creator of the Claude chatbot worth it? Will customers get enough value from its products to pay prices that justify that valuation? Is confidence in AI moving faster than companies’ ability to capitalize on it? After all, there are two ways to vote on AI: Buy the stock or buy the product. The first tells us how much capital investors are willing to commit. The second tells us whether customers get enough value to keep paying.

There are plenty of data points to discuss. Start with the org chart, which is the opposite of founder mode: CEO Dario Amodei has one direct report (Jensen Huang had 60 at Nvidia), with most of Anthropic’s senior team reporting to his sister, President Daniela Amodei. The average Anthropic employee is now worth more than $40 million . (Daniela, lunch is on you.) Anthropic’s novella-length list of risk factors about its products still reads like a dystopian sci-fi thriller . The company’s ownership structure, from the role of the Long-Term Benefit Trust to the Class F shares, can warm your heart and hurt your head. Who will decide when to speed up or slow down? 

For now, let’s look at this debut as both a bellwether of current AI sentiment and a…

items.title: Seed-oil-free foods are now a $1 billion business. Stanford scientists say the health claims don’t hold up
items.summary:
Walk down the snack aisle of almost any grocery store and you’ll find a growing number of packages labeled seed-oil-free. Americans bought more than $1 billion worth of seed-oil-free food products over the past year, according to NielsenIQ data.

Sales of seed-oil-free foods rose 60.2% over that period, while products without the label grew just 2.6%. Yet many nutrition and food scientists say those products aren’t necessarily healthier, and that seed oils aren’t harmful to people.

Seed oils are cooking oils extracted from crop seeds, including canola, corn, sunflower and safflower oil. Online influencers in the seed-oil-free movement, and the food companies serving this niche, push alternatives such as olive, avocado and coconut oil, along with animal fats like butter, lard and beef tallow, which has its own wave of celebrity backers .

Big food makers have taken notice. PepsiCo , the maker of Lay’s and Tostitos, said in 2025 that it would expand its use of avocado and olive oil in place of canola and soybean oil, one of several moves by food companies to rework products and keep up with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vision of a healthy diet .

A seal for a growing niche 

Many seed-oil-free packages carry a Seed Oil Free Certified seal. The Seed Oil Free Alliance, a Florida-based organization founded in 2023, issues it and audits products and lab-tests their oils. The alliance says products carrying its seal account for about $410 million in retail sales, citing NielsenIQ data.

“Our organization doesn’t fearmonger about seed oils,” Jonathan Rubin, the…
items.t: Seed-oil-free foods are now a $1 billion business. Stanford scientists say the health claims don’t hold up

items.title: French AI company Mistral picks Singapore for its Asia-Pacific headquarters, bringing Europe’s ‘sovereign AI’ pitch to China’s backyard
items.summary:
Mistral is opening its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore and plans to double its regional headcount to 200 by 2027, in a bet on regional interest in open-weight models. 

Chinese open-weight models—which are free for anyone to download and run on their own hardware—are already widely used in Southeast Asia. Singapore’s national AI R&D program built its latest SEA-LION model on Alibaba’s Qwen, while Singapore’s OCBC runs more than 30 internal banking tools on open models, including DeepSeek.

But Mistral thinks it can compete with Chinese providers by offering companies hands-on support. Marjorie Janiewicz, the company’s chief revenue officer, highlights three components to how to deliver an AI model: “There’s the intelligence. There’s the technology underneath to deploy it and the technology above to turn it into workflows and applications. And finally, the third component is forward-deployed engineering,” she explains.

When it comes to Chinese AI models, “usually we find that one, or multiple, of those components are missing to really get these companies to production,” she says.

Mistral’s Singapore office will also serve as an “extended Science Hub,” where the company will develop frontier models for the region’s public sector, as well as its high-tech manufacturing and robotics industries. 

“Over 70% of our team here is forward deployed engineers and scientists,” Geoff Soon, Mistral’s vice president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, says. “We’re very focused on building a deep scientific core in Singapore,” noting that almost all of their recent hires were in science…

items.title: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table
items.summary:
The Anthropic IPO just delivered Wall Street’s AI bulls a strong vote of confidence. The Claude-purveyor’s big jump on its opening day of trading for now dispelled fears that investors’ faith in the profitability of this era’s signature technology was fading. 

Here’s an issue that the bulls are ignoring, and that’s getting virtually no coverage in the media: Anthropic left an enormous share of the IPO’s proceeds on the table. We’re talking about roughly $20 billion that could have flowed into spending on AI infrastructure that instead went to big institutions, and privileged retail investors, that reaped a gigantic, one-day windfall, as well as the underwriters that will feast on big commissions they’ll receive from the clients they awarded shares at what looks like bargain prices.

The “left on the table” phenomenon looks amazingly like the scenario surrounding the SpaceX debut in June, though all told, the Anthropic forgone funding number’s even bigger. So let’s start by comparing the two offerings. In total amount raised, Anthropic edged SpaceX as the biggest IPO of all time, collecting a headline, gross amount from the shares sold to the public of $81.34 billion versus $75 billion for SpaceX.

For additional insights into the similarities and contrasts between the two IPOs, I spoke to Jay Ritter, professor at the University of Florida and the world’s leading expert in the field. First, Ritter noted that the percentage fees paid the underwriters are the two lowest numbers he’s ever witnessed, chiefly because the deals are so immense that even at what sounds like a tiny…
items.t: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table

items.title: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year
items.summary:
The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now . But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.

Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.

“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The chaos ends now, Smartex hopes. 

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary codesigner of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at…
items.t: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year

Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his…
items.t: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
